title: How much of an open-source chip design search can cheap fidelity rungs and proof prediction save, with a guarantee?
lede: milestones 1 to 3 done: on 10 designs x 60 ABC pass sequences, the generic-gate score does not rank like routed SKY130 area x delay (tau-b median -0.04), and liberty mapping mis-ranks too when the clock is tight (tau 0.59); at equal wall-clock a one-shot cheap-rung screen does not beat random or hill-climbing search on the cached table; successive halving across rungs does not beat random routed search on mean regret either (plain halving from the generic-gate rung is worst; a 6-point routed pilot to pick the start rung fixes most of that, H3), a 10-point routed pilot plus a conformal bound on the mapped rung keeps the routed optimum 0.99 of the time (nominal 0.90) at 42 to 57% of the routed runs, but on the generic-gate rung coverage fails (0.65 against 0.80, H4 refuted there); proof prediction (H5) not yet run
summary: An open research programme; milestone 1 is measured. Over 10 small designs, 60 ABC pass sequences each and two clock targets (1,200 runs through Yosys, ABC and OpenROAD on SKY130 HD), the generic-gate rung's Kendall tau-b against routed (global-route plus timing repair) area × period is below 0.7 on all 9 designs where it is defined (median −0.04), and its pick costs a median 13.5% of routed area × period. The liberty-mapped rung is no better than 0.59 median tau at a tight clock (median regret 10.5%) but nearly exact at a relaxed one (0% regret), because timing repair reorders designs. Routed points cost about 8× a generic point here, so there is little to save on designs this small. Limits: one corner and utilisation, global-route estimates, ten small designs. Milestone 2 replays search on the cached table at equal wall-clock: screening the pool at the generic-gate or mapped rung and verifying the top points does not beat random or hill-climbing search (45 s: regret 1.08% and 1.27% against 0.94% and 0.61%), and loses badly at smaller budgets. Hypotheses H2 to H5 (multi-fidelity wins, coverage, proof prediction) are not yet run. Milestone 3 replays successive halving across the four rungs: starting from the generic-gate rung it is the worst strategy (about 10% mean routed regret at the tight clock at 45 s against 0.94% for random search); starting at the mapped rung wins on most designs at a relaxed clock but loses heavily on two; a 6-point routed pilot that picks the start rung recovers the designs plain halving loses (H3), so there is no multi-fidelity gain at equal wall-clock on this 50-point pool yet. Milestone 4 (H4) replays conformal shortlists: a routed pilot of 10 to 16 points calibrates a one-sided bound on routed area × delay from a cheap rung. On the mapped rung the routed optimum is kept 0.99 of the time at nominal 0.90 (0.90–0.92 at 0.80) while routing 42–57% of the pool, against 0.53–0.65 for random search with equal routed runs; on the generic-gate rung coverage is 0.65 at nominal 0.80, no better than random search, so H4 is refuted there. Limits: 20 groups from 10 small designs, one corner.
